s: Oldacre's will made McFarlane the recipient of his property, subject to some reservations. Lestrade regards this inheritance as a motive for murder, while Holmes notes that the timing makes the alleged crime seem too obvious.

s: The evidence includes McFarlane's presence at Oldacre's house, the will benefiting him, blood-stains in the room and on his walking stick, and the burned body. Lestrade considers the evidence strongly favorable to his theory, but Holmes points out that it may also fit other explanations.

s: Sherlock Holmes investigates the apparent murder and disappearance of Jonas Oldacre, beginning at Blackheath and then examining Deep Dene House in Norwood. Evidence, including burned remains, Oldacre's trouser buttons, blood, and John McFarlane's thumbprint, appears to establish McFarlane's guilt, but Holmes notices inconsistencies. Holmes stages a fire alarm using burning straw, causing Jonas Oldacre to emerge from a concealed room. Oldacre is revealed to be alive and is taken into custody, while Inspector Lestrade acknowledges that Holmes has saved McFarlane from being wrongly hanged.

s: John McFarlane is accused of murdering Jonas Oldacre, with his walking stick, footprints, and apparent right-thumb bloodprint used against him. Holmes's discovery that Oldacre is alive shows that McFarlane's apparent guilt was based on a false interpretation of the evidence.

l: the police, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, When the detective departed, my friend rose and made his

s: The third dancing-men message appears two mornings later on the tool-house door. It is represented in the text as "COME-ELSIE," and Holmes is pleased that the evidence is accumulating.

s: The fourth dancing-men message is added by the unknown figure beneath an earlier arrangement on a different panel of the tool-house door. It is represented in the text as "NEVER," and Holmes considers its separate placement especially important.

l: the final dancing-men message, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE DANCING MEN
s: The final dancing-men message appears on the pedestal of the sundial after a period of quiet. It reads "ELSIE-PREPARE-TO-MEET-THY-GOD," causing Holmes alarm and prompting him to seek the earliest train to Norfolk.

l: the unknown dancing-men sender, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE DANCING MEN
s: The unknown dancing-men sender leaves messages secretly at night and is seen by Hilton Cubitt as a dark figure moving near the tool-house. The sender escapes before Cubitt can catch him, while Elsie Patrick appears to know who he is.

l: Hilton Cubitt's family honour, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE DANCING MEN
s: Hilton Cubitt places great importance on his family's long-standing reputation and unsullied honour. Elsie Patrick refers to this pride when she struggles to discuss the circumstances of her past.

l: Elsie Patrick's past, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE DANCING MEN
s: Elsie Patrick tells Hilton Cubitt that she has had disagreeable associations in her life but says she has nothing of which she is personally ashamed. She asks him to accept her word and allow her to remain silent about everything before their marriage.

l: the American associations, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE DANCING MEN
s: The American associations are connected with Elsie Patrick's undisclosed past. A letter bearing an American stamp makes her turn deadly white, and she burns it without explaining its contents.

l: the investigation, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE DANCING MEN
s: The investigation begins when Hilton Cubitt brings the dancing-men mystery to Sherlock Holmes. Holmes gathers copies of the messages, questions Cubitt about strangers and the sender, studies the figures, seeks information by telegram, and prepares to travel to Norfolk because the threat has become urgent.

l: The Return of Sherlock Holmes, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, So, indeed, it proved, and as I come to the dark conclusion of a
s: Sherlock Holmes and Dr. Watson travel to Riding Thorpe Manor after learning that Hilton Cubitt and his wife, Elsie Cubitt, have been shot. Holmes determines that a third shot was fired through the study window and finds evidence that a third person was present. By deciphering the dancing men messages, Holmes identifies Abe Slaney as the threatening correspondent and learns that he is a dangerous Chicago criminal. Holmes sends a note to Slaney at Elrige’s Farm and helps Inspector Martin organize the investigation.

l: Sherlock Holmes, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, So, indeed, it proved, and as I come to the dark conclusion of a
s: Sherlock Holmes travels to Riding Thorpe Manor with Dr. Watson, intending to prevent the threatened tragedy, but arrives after Hilton Cubitt has been killed and his wife has been seriously wounded. He examines the scene, identifies a third bullet and cartridge, reconstructs the likely presence of a person outside the window, and deciphers the dancing men messages. He sends a note to Abe Slaney at Elrige’s Farm and advises Inspector Martin to arrange an escort for Slaney.

l: Dr. Watson, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, So, indeed, it proved, and as I come to the dark conclusion of a
s: Dr. Watson accompanies Sherlock Holmes to Riding Thorpe Manor and observes Holmes’s investigation. He listens as Holmes explains the solution of the dancing men cipher and the events leading to the shooting.

l: Inspector Martin, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, So, indeed, it proved, and as I come to the dark conclusion of a
s: Inspector Martin of the Norfolk Constabulary is investigating the shooting at Riding Thorpe Manor when Holmes arrives. He agrees to work with Holmes, records the evidence, examines the premises with him, and is advised to arrange an escort for the suspected prisoner.

l: Hilton Cubitt, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, So, indeed, it proved, and as I come to the dark conclusion of a
s: Hilton Cubitt is found dead in the study at Riding Thorpe Manor after being shot through the heart. His body shows no powder-marking, and Holmes concludes that he was likely shot by a third person who had been outside the study window.

l: Mrs. Hilton Cubitt, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, So, indeed, it proved, and as I come to the dark conclusion of a
s: Elsie Cubitt, Hilton Cubitt’s wife, is found gravely wounded near the study window and is taken to her room for medical attention. The country surgeon reports that a bullet has passed through the front of her brain, though her injuries are not necessarily fatal. The dancing men messages reveal that Abe Slaney repeatedly appealed to her and threatened her.

l: Abe Slaney, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, So, indeed, it proved, and as I come to the dark conclusion of a
s: Abe Slaney is identified as the writer of the dancing men messages and as the person who had been communicating with Elsie Cubitt. Holmes learns from Wilson Hargreave that Slaney is known as the most dangerous crook in Chicago, and he sends a note summoning him at Elrige’s Farm.

l: Riding Thorpe Manor, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, So, indeed, it proved, and as I come to the dark conclusion of a
s: Riding Thorpe Manor is the scene of the shooting involving Hilton Cubitt and Elsie Cubitt. Its study contains the bodies, the revolver, a bullet hole through the window-sash, and evidence that a third person stood outside during the shooting.

l: Elrige’s Farm, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, So, indeed, it proved, and as I come to the dark conclusion of a
s: Elrige’s Farm is identified as a lonely farm near East Ruston where Abe Slaney is believed to be staying. Holmes sends a mounted boy there with a note addressed to Slaney.

l: the dancing-men cipher, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, So, indeed, it proved, and as I come to the dark conclusion of a
s: The dancing men cipher uses childlike figures to represent letters, with flags apparently separating words. Holmes deciphers the messages as communications involving Elsie and Abe Slaney, including phrases such as “AM HERE ABE SLANEY,” “COME ELSIE,” and “ELSIE PREPARE TO MEET THY GO[ D].”

l: the shooting at Riding Thorpe Manor, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, So, indeed, it proved, and as I come to the dark conclusion of a
s: The shooting occurs at about three in the morning, killing Hilton Cubitt and seriously wounding Elsie Cubitt. Two shots are heard, but Holmes finds evidence of a third shot fired through the study window, indicating that another person was present. The window was open during the shooting and later shut and fastened from inside.

l: the investigation, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, So, indeed, it proved, and as I come to the dark conclusion of a
s: The investigation is conducted by Inspector Martin with Sherlock Holmes’s assistance. It examines the servants’ testimony, the bodies, the study, the window, the garden footprints, the revolver, the third cartridge, and the dancing men messages. Holmes concludes that the evidence points toward Abe Slaney.

l: the revolver, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, So, indeed, it proved, and as I come to the dark conclusion of a
s: The revolver is found on the study floor midway between Hilton Cubitt and Elsie Cubitt, with two barrels discharged and two cartridges remaining. Holmes finds the ejected third cartridge in the garden and uses the bullet hole in the window-sash to establish that a third shot was fired.

l: the note to Abe Slaney, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, So, indeed, it proved, and as I come to the dark conclusion of a
s: The note to Abe Slaney is written by Sherlock Holmes using the dancing men symbols and addressed to “Mr. Abe Slaney, Elriges Farm, East Ruston.” Holmes sends it with a boy instructed to deliver it directly to Slaney and answer no questions.

l: The Return of Sherlock Holmes, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, “It is a privilege to be associated with you in the handling of a
s: Sherlock Holmes and Inspector Martin arrest Abe Slaney after Holmes lures him to the house with a coded note. Slaney confesses that he confronted Hilton Cubitt over Mrs. Hilton Cubitt, that Cubitt fired first, and that Slaney then shot him and fled. Holmes establishes that Mrs. Hilton Cubitt was not responsible for her husband's death and that Slaney's threats and pursuit drove the tragedy. Slaney is later sentenced to death, with the penalty commuted to penal servitude, while Mrs. Hilton Cubitt recovers.

l: Sherlock Holmes, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, “It is a privilege to be associated with you in the handling of a
s: Sherlock Holmes writes a coded invitation to Abe Slaney, anticipates that Slaney will come, and directs Inspector Martin to arrest him. He explains the dancing-men cipher, establishes that Mrs. Hilton Cubitt was not responsible for her husband's death, and uses Slaney's confession to clarify the case.

l: Dr. Watson, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, “It is a privilege to be associated with you in the handling of a
s: Dr. Watson observes Holmes and Inspector Martin's arrest of Abe Slaney and listens to Slaney's confession. Holmes asks him to read the decoy note, which contains the message COME-HERE-AT-ONCE.

l: Inspector Martin, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, “It is a privilege to be associated with you in the handling of a
s: Inspector Martin worries that he will be blamed if Abe Slaney escapes, then helps Sherlock Holmes arrest Slaney by placing handcuffs on him. He warns Slaney that his statement may be used against him and later takes him to Norwich.

l: Abe Slaney, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, “It is a privilege to be associated with you in the handling of a
s: Abe Slaney comes to the house in response to Holmes's coded note and is arrested by Holmes and Inspector Martin. He says that Hilton Cubitt fired first during a confrontation and that Slaney then shot him, while denying that he harmed Mrs. Hilton Cubitt. He is later condemned to death, but his penalty is changed to penal servitude because of mitigating circumstances and the certainty that Hilton Cubitt fired first.

l: Mrs. Hilton Cubitt, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, “It is a privilege to be associated with you in the handling of a
s: Mrs. Hilton Cubitt is found badly wounded beside her dead husband and is initially near death. Abe Slaney insists that he loved her and did not harm her, while Holmes states that Slaney's pursuit and threats drove her to attempt suicide. She later recovers entirely and devotes her life to caring for the poor and administering her husband's estate.

l: Hilton Cubitt, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, “It is a privilege to be associated with you in the handling of a
s: Hilton Cubitt confronts Abe Slaney after finding him with Mrs. Hilton Cubitt and fires the first shot. Slaney returns fire, killing Hilton Cubitt.

l: the case concerning the Cubitts' shooting, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, “It is a privilege to be associated with you in the handling of a
s: The case concerns the shooting of Hilton Cubitt and the serious wounding of Mrs. Hilton Cubitt, with Abe Slaney initially suspected of murder. Holmes resolves the central uncertainty by arresting Slaney and obtaining his account, which clears Mrs. Hilton Cubitt of responsibility and identifies Slaney as the surviving gunman.

l: Hilton Cubitt's shooting and death, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, “It is a privilege to be associated with you in the handling of a
s: Hilton Cubitt is shot and killed during his confrontation with Abe Slaney. Slaney claims that Cubitt fired first and that his own shot was therefore not murder, a circumstance later treated as mitigating.

l: Mrs. Hilton Cubitt's shooting and attempted suicide, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, “It is a privilege to be associated with you in the handling of a
s: Mrs. Hilton Cubitt is found badly wounded beside Hilton Cubitt's body and is believed to have attempted suicide after his death. Holmes says that Slaney's pursuit, threats, and actions brought about the tragedy, and she eventually recovers entirely.

l: Abe Slaney's arrest, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, “It is a privilege to be associated with you in the handling of a
s: Sherlock Holmes lures Abe Slaney to the house with a coded note, where Holmes puts a pistol to his head and Inspector Martin handcuffs him. Slaney is then taken by cab to Norwich.

l: the dancing-men cipher, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, “It is a privilege to be associated with you in the handling of a
s: The dancing-men cipher was invented by Mrs. Hilton Cubitt's father, Patrick, who was the leader of a gang in Chicago. It appears as a child's scrawl unless the key is known, and Holmes uses it to communicate with Abe Slaney.

l: the note to Abe Slaney, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, “It is a privilege to be associated with you in the handling of a
s: Holmes's decoy note uses the dancing-men cipher to invite Abe Slaney to come to the house. Holmes believes Slaney will trust it because he will assume that only Mrs. Hilton Cubitt could have written it.

l: the message COME-HERE-AT-ONCE, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, “It is a privilege to be associated with you in the handling of a
s: COME-HERE-AT-ONCE is the coded message written on Holmes's decoy note. Using the dancing-men cipher, it means 'Come here at once' and successfully brings Abe Slaney to the house.

l: The Return of Sherlock Holmes, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE SOLITARY CYCLIST
s: The unit introduces the case of Violet Smith, a music teacher who seeks Sherlock Holmes's advice after being repeatedly followed by a bearded cyclist on the lonely road near Charlington Heath. Violet explains that Mr. Carruthers hired her to teach his daughter at Chiltern Grange, while Mr. Woodley later assaulted her and was driven away by Carruthers. Holmes suspects that the pursuer may be connected to Charlington Hall and questions the relationship between Carruthers and Woodley, as well as their search for Violet's uncle, Ralph Smith. Holmes sends Watson to investigate the road and the occupants of Charlington Hall.

l: Sherlock Holmes, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE SOLITARY CYCLIST
s: Sherlock Holmes interviews Violet Smith about the cyclist who follows her and deduces details about her bicycling, music teaching, and circumstances. He notices that the pursuer disappears near Charlington Hall, suspects a connection involving Mr. Carruthers and Mr. Woodley, and sends Watson to investigate.

l: Dr. Watson, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE SOLITARY CYCLIST
s: Watson records the case and observes Holmes's examination of Violet Smith. Holmes instructs Watson to hide near Charlington Heath on Monday, observe the cyclist, and inquire about the occupants of Charlington Hall.

l: Violet Smith, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE SOLITARY CYCLIST
s: Violet Smith is a young music teacher who works at Chiltern Grange and travels by bicycle between the house and Farnham Station. She reports that a middle-aged, dark-bearded man repeatedly follows her on a bicycle near Charlington Heath, and she asks Holmes for advice.

l: Ralph Smith, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE SOLITARY CYCLIST
s: Ralph Smith is Violet Smith's uncle, who went to Africa twenty-five years earlier and had not contacted Violet or her mother. After his death in Johannesburg, he supposedly asked Mr. Carruthers and Mr. Woodley to find his relations and ensure that they were not in want.

l: Mr. Carruthers, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE SOLITARY CYCLIST
s: Mr. Carruthers is a South African acquaintance of Ralph Smith who hires Violet Smith to teach his ten-year-old daughter at Chiltern Grange. He is described as an older, polite, musical widower, and he intervenes when Mr. Woodley assaults Violet; Violet also suspects that Carruthers takes a personal interest in her.

l: Mr. Woodley, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE SOLITARY CYCLIST
s: Mr. Woodley is a coarse, red-moustached man who returned from South Africa with Mr. Carruthers. He makes unwanted advances to Violet Smith, seizes her, and is knocked down and driven away after Carruthers intervenes; Holmes also considers his connection with Carruthers suspicious.

l: the cyclist pursuing Miss Smith, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE SOLITARY CYCLIST
s: The solitary cyclist's pursuer appears repeatedly behind Violet Smith on the road near Charlington Heath. He rides a bicycle, wears a dark suit and cloth cap, has a short dark beard, keeps his distance, and disappears near a sharp turn without using any visible side road.

l: Charlington, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE SOLITARY CYCLIST
s: Charlington is associated with the isolated road and the grounds of Charlington Hall where Violet Smith encounters the cyclist pursuing her.

l: Charlington Heath, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE SOLITARY CYCLIST
s: Charlington Heath lies beside the lonely road Violet Smith uses to reach Farnham Station. Holmes identifies it as the place where Watson should conceal himself to observe the pursuer.
